claims.text: The starting single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC crystal structure.
Annealing removes residual stresses while retaining point defects and surface steps, with no precipitates or grain boundaries present.
Yielding is initiated predominantly by thermally activated dislocation nucleation rather than motion of pre-existing dislocations.
Surface steps, vacancies, and intrinsic stacking faults act as preferential dislocation-nucleation sites.
Severe lattice distortion produces substantial local stacking-fault-energy variability and high Peierls-like barriers for dislocation nucleation.
High configurational entropy and atomic-size mismatch create a high dislocation-nucleation energy barrier in FCC HEAs.
Between 300 K and 600 K, thermal activation assists the alloy in overcoming the dislocation-nucleation barrier.
Thermally activated nucleation produces only weak yield-strength dependence on strain rate from 300 K to 600 K.
The activation energy for dislocation nucleation is approximately 0.5–0.8 eV.
At 77 K, suppression of thermal activation causes a transition to athermal nucleation at the most favorable defects.
At 77 K, yield strength increases by more than 30% relative to higher-temperature behavior.
At 77 K, yield strength becomes highly sensitive to strain rate.
FCC-to-BCC transformation is not the primary deformation mode during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
FCC-to-BCC transformation is energetically less favorable than FCC-to-HCP transformation or deformation twinning in this composition range.
FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation or deformation twinning occurs only after yielding.
A high initial density of pre-existing dislocations shifts the controlling mechanism from nucleation to dislocation glide.
The shift to dislocation glide at high initial dislocation density significantly increases strain-rate sensitivity.
Loading along [111] or [100] maximizes crystal-orientation anisotropy effects.
Traditional FCC metals such as Cu and Al have highly strain-rate-sensitive yield strength because dislocation glide is rate limiting.
Traditional FCC metals lack a significant dislocation-nucleation barrier when pre-existing dislocations are absent.

contradictions.description: The cryogenic regime is described as athermal nucleation, yet it is also predicted to become highly strain-rate sensitive. The hypothesis does not provide an additional rate-dependent process that reconciles strong rate sensitivity with the asserted athermal control.
